newsitem.title: PERU: Tokyo envoy heads to Cuba seeking Lima crisis end.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo envoy heads to Cuba seeking Lima crisis end.

text.p: Japan's Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura left on Wednesday for Cuba, the next stop in his search for a peaceful solution to the Lima hostage crisis now into its fourth month.

Japanese diplomatic sources said Komura would meet President Fidel Castro in Havana on Wednesday evening to formalise a request from Tokyo that Cuba give asylum to Peru's Marxist rebel hostage-takers if a negotiated solution is reached.

Castro has told Peru's President Alberto Fujimori that Cuba would be prepared to take the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels holding 72 captives in the Japanese ambassador's residence for 92 days. But Tokyo must endorse any such deal.

Komura spent two days in Lima cautioning Peru's government against using force to end the siege and pressing for a speedy settlement. Talks are stuck over the MRTA's central demand for the release of some 450 jailed comrades.

"It has been a very successful visit. We have confirmed our joint commitment to looking for an early and peaceful solution," a senior Japanese diplomat in Lima told Reuters. "We have asked the Peruvian government to do everything possible to speed up the talks process. Already three months have passed, so we have to finish this issue as soon as possible."

Komura, who was due to arrive in Havana at 5 p.m. (2200 GMT), was to travel on Thurday to the Dominican Republic, which like Cuba has offered asylum for some of the MRTA members. Despite the diplomatic moves, the MRTA has given no indication it will accept asylum or end its siege with anything less than the release of its jailed members.

Fujimori has rejected that demand but he is believed to be considering concessions such as improving harsh jail conditions for rebels convicted of terrorism or releasing a small number of MRTA rebels not yet sentenced or convicted on lesser charges.

With attention focused on Komura's visit, Peru's military announced late on Tuesday the capture of 38 "MRTA terrorists" during a sweep of the group's eastern jungle stronghold. The Armed Forces Joint Command said the rebels planned to attack an army base in Oxapampa, some 200 miles (325 kms) east of Lima.

"A tough blow has been dealt to the MRTA terrorist organisation, preventing it from continuing the violent activities, robberies, lootings and thefts it was carrying out in the zone," it said in a statement.

Villagers said the army had detained peasants unconnected to the MRTA, killing one man and torturing others. The armed forces statement, however, said the operation was carried out "with complete respect for human rights."
The army did not say when the suspects were caught but as late as Sunday the rebels said none of their members were detained despite a major offensive to flush them out.

There was calm on Wednesday at the site of the besieged residence in the upscale San Isidro district of Lima. Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer sought to reassure family members increasingly worried about the hostages, mainly middle-aged and suffering a range of stress, skin, stomach and other illnesses.
"There is much serenity and calm, which is good from the mental and physical point of view," he said. "There is permanent care (from medical teams) for the people who suffer chronic illnesses."
